title: [PLACEHOLDER] Ethical Hacking: The Foundations
content:
[PLACEHOLDER] Ethical hacking is the practice of deliberately probing computer systems, networks, and applications for security vulnerabilities — with explicit written permission from the owner.

The goal is identical to a malicious attacker's: find weaknesses. The difference is what happens after discovery. An ethical hacker documents and reports findings so they can be fixed. A criminal exploits them for profit or disruption.

Ethical hackers operate under three core constraints:
- **Written authorisation** — always documented in a formal contract
- **Defined scope** — clear boundaries on what can and cannot be tested
- **No data retention** — discovered data is handled under strict confidentiality

callouts.title: [PLACEHOLDER] Key Distinction
callouts.text: [PLACEHOLDER] Ethical hacking (also called penetration testing or pen testing) is authorised. Any hacking without explicit permission is illegal, regardless of intent.

callouts.title: [PLACEHOLDER] Legal Reality
callouts.text: [PLACEHOLDER] In most countries, unauthorised access to computer systems is a criminal offence — even if you discover vulnerabilities and report them. Always obtain written permission first.

keyTerms.definition: [PLACEHOLDER] A simulated cyberattack against a system to evaluate its security posture. Also called a pen test.
[PLACEHOLDER] Vulnerability Assessment and Penetration Testing — a combined methodology that identifies and validates security weaknesses.
[PLACEHOLDER] The explicitly defined boundaries of a penetration test — which systems, IP ranges, and attack techniques are permitted.
